Archie vs an agent on a cloud computer.

With Archie, your agent works on the computer you own, signed into your accounts from your own desk. Compare that with Dots, Cowork, Grok Bot, Symphony, Muse and Cue.

Wix and Manus do not say where their agents runSource 8Source 17.

Archie is in testing. Where it stands → Checked against the sources below on August 20, 2026, September 11 for Symphony, September 15 for Muse, September 29 for Cue, and September 30 for Dots.

Whose computer

Your computer is the one you can switch off.

Where Archie wins

Your accounts, AI choice and approval stay in your hands.

Connect from your own desk

Your agent works on your computer, with account tokens in its password storeSource 5. What you ask it still goes to an AI company’s computers.

Choose which AI answers

Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq, xAI, DeepSeek or Mistral, on your own account, switchable whenever you likeSource 5. The app estimates usage; the AI company’s dashboard has the billSource 6.

Review email replies and calendar changes

A calendar change waits for approval in a later message. An email reply waits until you send it or set a time. Neither gate can be turned offSource 5. Read each proposal before approving it.

Where cloud agents win

A cloud computer keeps working while yours is off.

Leave your laptop shut

Dots keep working when your computer is offSource 18. A Grok Bot runs on a persistent cloud computerSource 3. Archie needs your computer awake; a timed routine can wake it once set up.

Use a plan you already have

Cowork comes with Claude ProSource 1 and Dots with ChatGPT ProSource 18. Symphony offers a free plan with credits that reset monthlySource 9.

Take calls through your agent

Dots can answer a callSource 18. Cue agents have their own phone numbers and can take calls and leave summariesSource 17. Archie makes no phone calls.

Prices and sources

Check what each plan and each piece of work costs.

Archie is free at 20 jobs a day on your own AI account, or $30 a month without the limitSource 6. AI usage is extra: $1 to $5 a month for light use; heavier use costs moreSource 6.

Our free starting credits pass through our server on the way to Anthropic while we are payingSource 5. Email features need an AI account of your own.

Check the AI cost per reply, credit or action
What one unit of AI work costs on each agent, in that agent’s own unit, from its own price list, beside Archie’s measured cost per reply.
Agent Their unit What it costs
Archie One reply from your agent, with every pass it takes inside it $0.01 when it follows another closely, up to $0.11 when it starts from nothing, measured on an agent with twelve add-ons and everything connected, at BalancedSource 6. A reply that hands work to a specialist or uses the Deep setting costs more. Billed by the AI company to you
Lindy A credit. An “everyday ask” is 2 to 250 of them, “deep work” 250 to 1,000 $29.99 a month for 3,000 credits, so an everyday ask is $0.02 to $2.50 and deep work $2.50 to $10Source 10
Zapier Agents An activity: one action, one search, or one question answered from a knowledge source $400 a year for 1,500 activities a month, about $0.02 eachSource 11
Microsoft Copilot Studio A credit. An answer is 2 of them, an action 5 $200 a month for 25,000 credits, or $0.01 each pay as you go, so a reply that takes two actions is about $0.10 to $0.12Source 12
Salesforce Agentforce A conversation, or an action paid in Flex Credits $2 a conversation, or $0.10 an actionSource 13
Claude Code, an agent on a key like ours A developer’s working day About $13 an active day and $150 to $250 a month, on Anthropic’s own figuresSource 14

Read each row in its own unit: a Lindy credit, a Copilot credit and a reply are different sizes of work, and the companies say so. Ours is one reply with everything it did inside it; most of theirs is one step.

Claude Code is a coding agent, which works a problem far harder than an assistant does. It is here because it is the same kind of bill as ours: an agent on your own key, priced by the AI company. One person’s published three-month log of OpenClaw, another agent on a key, came to $187, $94 and $78 a month as its owner moved to cheaper modelsSource 15.

Their prices checked September 12, 2026; Archie measured in August and priced September 12.

Sources for every figure and claim on this page
1Claude Cowork, on paid Claude plans

Anthropic’s pricing page, claude.com/pricing, lists “Includes Claude Cowork” on the Pro card, $20 a month or $17 billed annually, read on August 20, 2026. The permission modes, including Skip (“Claude doesn’t pause to ask and nothing checks its actions automatically”), are in Anthropic’s own guide.

2Where Cowork runs

“Claude’s work runs on Anthropic’s servers, in an isolated environment, and your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account”. From Anthropic’s getting-started guide, read on August 20, 2026, which also lists where Cowork is available: the Claude desktop, web and mobile apps.

3Grok Bot

In beta on desktop and iOS. Each Bot “runs on a persistent cloud VM with a browser, filesystem, and terminal”, signs in to your tools there, and comes back “when something needs your approval”. From xAI’s announcement and its documentation, read on August 20, 2026.

4Grok Bot’s prices

SuperGrok Heavy at $300 a month and Cursor Ultra at $200 a month, from the Grok Bot plan cards, read in a browser and transcribed on August 20, 2026. Those pages refuse automated requests, so this is the one set of figures here no script of ours can re-check. The same cards list Cursor Teams Premium at $120 a seat.

5Archie’s side of the table

The custody claim, the password-store claim, the 7 providers, the 5 chat apps and the approval gate are all on our Trust page. It lists everything Archie sends and to whom, and shows how to watch it yourself with a network monitor.

6Archie, $30 a month, and the $1 to $5

Our own price, and our own measured figure for light AI use (a handful of tasks a day), both broken down on the pricing page. Heavier use costs more. The app keeps an estimate as you go, and the AI company’s own dashboard has the real bill.

7The final-build commitment

Our Terms require us to publish a version that needs no license check if we cease operating. The wording is in the Terms of Service and the reasoning is on the Trust page.

8Symphony by Wix, and where it runs

An AI agent platform for small businesses with a “mobile-first interface”. “Symphony is available on iOS and Android. Download the app and take your business with you wherever you go”, and it runs in a browser too; you use it with a Wix account, though it needs no Wix website.

It is “powered by Wix AI and built on 20 years of real business expertise”, and the page names no model and offers no model choice. Wix does not publish where the agents run, so neither do we: we say how you reach it, which is what their pages state. From wix.com/symphony and the Symphony overview, read on September 11, 2026.

9Symphony’s prices and its credits

Free, then Basic at $16 a month ($12.80 billed annually), Pro at $40 ($32) and Max at $80 ($64). The free plan needs no credit card and carries 500 monthly credits and 100 daily credits; credits “reset monthly and do not roll over”. Basic carries 2,000 monthly credits and Pro 5,000; Max publishes no figure.

The unit is defined on the page as: “Each action you take with agents and tools consumes AI credits. The exact amount is calculated after each action, based on its complexity and the tool used.” From wix.com/symphony/pricing, read on September 11, 2026. The daily cap was 50 when this page was first written and is 100 now, so the figure above is the one re-read on that date.

10Lindy’s credits

Plus at $29.99 a month per user with “3k credits / user / mo”, from lindy.ai/pricing, and the ranges “Everyday Asks 2-250 Credits” and “Deep work 250-1,000 Credits” from the same page, read September 12, 2026. The per-ask dollars are our arithmetic on those two published numbers: $29.99 over 3,000 credits is a cent a credit.

11Zapier Agents’ activities

“Agents Pro $400 billed annually” with “up to 1,500 times per month”, from zapier.com/l/agents-pricing, read September 12, 2026. What counts as one activity is from Zapier’s help article: a trigger, an action, a search, a question answered from a knowledge source, each one activity. $400 over twelve months of 1,500 is 2.2 cents, our arithmetic.

12Microsoft Copilot Studio’s credits

“1 capacity pack = 25,000 Copilot Credits” at “$200 per credit pack/month (billed annually)” from Microsoft’s pricing page. The rate table, generative answer 2 credits and agent action 5, with the pay-as-you-go rate of $0.01 a credit, is from Microsoft Learn; both were read September 12, 2026. A reply that takes two actions is 12 credits, our arithmetic: $0.096 prepaid, $0.12 metered.

13Salesforce Agentforce’s conversations and actions

“$2 USD per conversation” and “$500 USD per 100,000 Credits” from salesforce.com/agentforce/pricing, and “One Agentforce action consumes 20 Flex Credits ($0.10 USD)” from Salesforce’s Flex Credits announcement, read September 12, 2026.

14What Claude Code costs, in Anthropic’s words

“Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month”, from code.claude.com/docs/en/costs, read September 12, 2026. A coding agent, not an assistant, and on the page for the shape of the bill rather than the size of the job.

15One person’s OpenClaw bill, three months running

A self-hosted OpenClaw agent tracked by its owner: “Month one: $187” on Claude Opus, $94 in month two after moving to Sonnet, and $78 in month three. From a dev.to post of March 30, 2026, read September 12, 2026. It is one person’s log, and it is the only kind of figure that exists for an open-source runner with no price of its own.

16Muse by Meta, and where it runs

Meta’s personal AI agent, announced on September 8, 2026. It “runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it”. It is “rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai, and coming soon to AI glasses”.

On approval, Meta’s help center says “By default, Muse will not take many important actions, like sending an email, without your approval”. On privacy, Meta says Muse “doesn’t share a person’s conversations or the data in their VM with Meta’s ad systems”. It adds that people “can opt out of their interactions being used to train Meta’s AI models”.

On price it says only that Muse is “free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more”. Meta publishes no figure we could read, so we print none. From Meta’s announcement, read on September 15, 2026.

17Cue by Manus, and what Manus says about it

Cue is “a new standalone app for your personal agents”, “built on the same infrastructure as Manus”. Each agent has “its own email, phone number, wallet, and computer, so it can send messages, pay within the budget you set, and see a task through on its own machine”. It “can also take your calls and leave you a summary in Cue”.

It is “in early access and free to use with an invite code”, on the web, desktop and mobile, with iOS to follow after App Store review. Of agents working together in a group chat, Manus says “You set the direction and make the final call.”

Manus does not say where an agent’s computer runs, and describes no approval step and no model for Cue, so we say none. From the Manus 2.0 announcement of September 28 and its help center, read on September 29, 2026.

18Dots by OpenAI, and where they run

OpenAI’s “always-on agents”, announced on September 29, 2026 and “Powered by GPT-6 Astra”. “Each dot works on its own cloud computer, while your computer and its contents stay separate unless you choose to connect it.” Connecting yours “is optional and starts turned off”. A dot “can keep working even when your computer is off”, and you reach it “in ChatGPT, Slack, Teams, or a call”.

On approval: “Dots start with built-in rules for when to act independently and when to ask for approval. Custom Rules let you allow specific actions, require approval, or block them.” One of those rules is “Take action without asking”. On training, OpenAI says it does not use content from Business, Enterprise or Edu workspaces to improve its models by default, and that personal plans can control it.

On price, OpenAI says “Your first dot is included in your Pro or Business Premium plan at no extra cost”. The Pro card on ChatGPT’s pricing page reads “From $100 / month” and lists “Dot, your always-on agent”. Pro users get it outside the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK. The plan “includes an allowance for deeper work” and OpenAI publishes no price per task.

From OpenAI’s announcement, ChatGPT’s guide to dots and its controls page, OpenAI’s help center and ChatGPT’s pricing page, read on September 30, 2026. Three of those refuse scripts, so we read them through a service that returns a page’s own text.

What we have not claimed

Nothing here says these products are careless with your content: each company documents its own isolation, defaults and approvals, and we quote them doing it. The claim is only about where the work happens: on a computer their company runs for four of them, somewhere Wix does not say for Symphony, and on yours for Archie.

Nothing here says Dots act without asking you. OpenAI publishes that they have built-in rules for when to ask, and does not list those rules.

For Cue, Manus says each agent has a computer of its own and does not say where. Nothing here says Cue acts without asking you, because Manus’s pages do not say either way.

Nothing here says Symphony trains on one customer’s data to answer another: we quote what Wix says its AI is drawn from, and nothing more. Each company’s own security documentation is the place to judge their side properly.
